input.text: This is Nanluoguxiang — an eight-hundred-year-old hutong from the Yuan dynasty, and one of the oldest alleys still standing in Beijing. Its name means "South Luogu Alley", and its layout is remarkable: the main alley runs about eight hundred meters north to south, with sixteen side hutongs branching out like the legs of a centipede — locals have called it "the Centipede Street" for centuries. This chessboard plan dates to the founding of Yuan-dynasty Dadu, the city that became modern Beijing. What makes it special is the mix: gray-brick courtyard homes — siheyuan — standing beside cafés, bakeries, and design shops. Each side hutong hides its own stories: former residences of generals, painters, and playwrights are marked with plaques as you wander. Go at a quiet hour if you can, and step into the side alleys — that's where the eight hundred years actually live.
